explanations.explanation: Simon of Cyrene, a man coming in from the country, gets the cross put on him to carry behind Jesus. The soldiers seized him, so this wasn't his idea. I think Simon woke up that morning with a totally different to-do list. Some days just grab you by the collar, friend.

Chains sound dramatic, but Luke never mentions any here. What the soldiers put on Simon of Cyrene was the cross, and he carried it behind Jesus. Simon was just a man on his way in from the country when they seized him.
No spears show up in this verse. The soldiers seized Simon of Cyrene, a man on his way in from the country, and put the cross on him. He carried it behind Jesus, and he didn't get a vote.

Jesus turns to these women, the daughters of Jerusalem, and says, “…do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.” Think about that. He's on His way to the cross, and He's still the one looking out for them. He doesn't say why He's telling them this, so I won't guess, but He sure doesn't brush them off.

Jesus doesn't name any leaders in this moment. He turns to the women and says, “…weep for yourselves and for your children.” He's talking straight to the ones in front of Him. Easy one to mix up, friend, because the rulers do show up later in the passage.

The women from Galilee do show up in this passage, but not here. Luke mentions them at the very end, standing at a distance. Here Jesus tells the weeping women, “…weep for yourselves and for your children.” He's pointing them back to their own homes and families.

Jesus says, “Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!” That's what people will say in the days He warns about. It's a strange thing to hear, and I think it tells us how heavy those days will be. He doesn't spell out more than that, so I'll leave it there.

You'd expect people to call that foolish, but Jesus says the opposite. He says people will declare, “Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!” Same words, flipped upside down from what we'd guess. That's what makes the warning stop you in your tracks.

Jesus never uses that word here. He says people will say, “Blessed are the barren women, the wombs that never bore, and breasts that never nursed!” It's a surprising thing to call someone blessed. I think that's the whole point of how serious the warning is.

Easy guess to make, friend, but Luke doesn't call these two disciples. He says they were criminals, led away to be executed with Jesus. The disciples aren't in this scene at all. Later in the passage, one of these two criminals has a lot to say.

Right, they aren't disciples. Luke says, “Two others, who were criminals, were also led away to be executed with Jesus.” So Jesus is walking this road with two criminals beside Him. And hold onto them, because one of those two ends up in a conversation you won't forget.

explanations.answer: One on His right and one on His left
explanations.explanation: At The Skull, they crucified Jesus “along with the criminals, one on His right and the other on His left.” So He has one criminal on each side. Luke doesn't tell us anything more about how they were arranged, so I won't add details. Remember those two, because they're about to matter.

explanations.answer: Both of them down the hill behind Him
explanations.explanation: Luke doesn't mention any hill or anybody being placed behind Him. He says the criminals were crucified there with Jesus, one on His right and the other on His left. They're right beside Him, and that matters later when one of them speaks up.

explanations.answer: Both of them together on His right
explanations.explanation: Close, because they are right next to Him. But Luke says one is on His right and the other on His left. Not both on one side. One criminal on each side, and both of them end up speaking before this is over.

explanations.answer: Forgive them because they don't know what they're doing
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” Look at where He is when He says it. He's hanging on a cross, and He prays for forgiveness. I think that's one of the most powerful lines in the whole passage.

explanations.answer: Judge them for everything they have done to Me
explanations.explanation: That's what most of us would say in His place, friend. But Jesus says the opposite: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” He asks for forgiveness. Not judgment.

explanations.answer: Take Me down from this cross before the night
explanations.explanation: Luke doesn't record Jesus asking for that. What He says is, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” His prayer is for the people around Him. I think that's worth sitting with.
Luke says they divided up His garments by casting lots. That's a way of settling who gets what. It happens right after Jesus prays for them to be forgiven.
Luke says the opposite: “And they divided up His garments by casting lots.” Casting lots was a way of deciding who got what. It comes right after Jesus asks His Father to forgive them.

explanations.answer: If You are the King of the Jews save Yourself
explanations.explanation: The soldiers say, “If You are the King of the Jews, save Yourself!” Sound familiar? The rulers sneered something close to it just a verse or two before. Same kind of taunt, and now it's coming from the soldiers too.

explanations.answer: If You are a prophet tell us who hit You
explanations.explanation: That's not what the soldiers say here. Luke 23:37 records them saying, “If You are the King of the Jews, save Yourself!” Their taunt is about being a king and saving Himself. It's a good reminder to listen closely to what the text actually says.

explanations.answer: If You are the Son of God call down fire
explanations.explanation: No fire talk in this scene, friend. The soldiers say, “If You are the King of the Jews, save Yourself!” Notice the title they use is King of the Jews. And the sign above Him uses the same title.

The second criminal says, “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment?” Look at that. He's hanging on a cross himself, and he still stops to correct the other man. I think a lot is changing in his heart right here.

explanations.answer: Whether he even knows who Jesus is
explanations.explanation: He doesn't put it that way. He asks, “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment?” He does speak about Jesus in the very next verse, though. There he says, “this man has done nothing wrong.”

explanations.answer: Whether he even hears the crowd
explanations.explanation: The crowd isn't what he's talking about. His question is, “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same judgment?” His words are aimed at the other criminal, and they're about God. The crowd barely comes into it.

He says, “We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve.” Notice he says we, so he's including himself. That takes honesty, especially on a day like that. Then he turns and speaks up for Jesus.

He actually says the opposite of what you'd expect from the False answer. His words are, “We are punished justly, for we are receiving what our actions deserve.” He's admitting it about himself and the other criminal. Then he says Jesus is different.

He says, “But this man has done nothing wrong.” He's just admitted that he and the other man deserve what they're getting. Then he turns around and says that about Jesus. It's a clear line between them.
He says the opposite. His words are, “But this man has done nothing wrong.” Nothing wrong, not nothing good. He's speaking up for Jesus from his own cross.
Useful isn't a word he reaches for. He says, “But this man has done nothing wrong.” He's talking about right and wrong, friend. And he's saying it while hanging next to Jesus.

Jesus tells him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” Hold on to the word today. The man asked to be remembered, and Jesus answers with a promise. I think that man heard more than he ever hoped to.
Jerusalem is where all this is happening, but it's not what Jesus promises. He says, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” Paradise is the word. And He says today.

Galilee comes up at the end of the passage, where the women who followed Jesus from there are watching. But it's not the promise. Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.” Paradise, and today.

explanations.answer: It is torn down the middle
explanations.explanation: Luke says the veil of the temple was torn down the middle. That happens right as the sun is darkened. Luke doesn't explain what it means in this passage, so I won't guess. I'll just say it's a big moment.
No fire in this verse, friend. Luke says the veil of the temple “was torn down the middle.” It's torn, not burned. That detail is easy to remember.

explanations.answer: It is rolled up and hidden
explanations.explanation: Nobody rolls anything up here. Luke says the veil of the temple “was torn down the middle.” It's torn right down the center. And Luke says it right alongside the sun being darkened.

explanations.answer: Into Your hands I commit My Spirit
explanations.explanation: Jesus calls out in a loud voice, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” Even now, He's talking to His Father. Then Luke says He breathed His last. I think this one deserves a quiet moment.

explanations.answer: Send Your angels to take Me down
explanations.explanation: Luke doesn't record Jesus saying that. In a loud voice, He says, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” He's speaking to His Father, and He's placing Himself in His Father's hands. Take a second with that.

explanations.answer: Let this darkness end right now
explanations.explanation: The darkness is there, but that's not what He asks. He calls out, “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.” He's speaking to His Father. And right after He says it, He breathes His last.

Luke says the centurion saw what happened and “gave glory to God.” He's a Roman army officer, and he's standing at a crucifixion. Then he says something about Jesus that nobody else around there says. I think that's a real surprise.
It's the opposite, friend. When the centurion saw what happened, he gave glory to God. A Roman army officer, in that spot, giving glory to God. Then he says what he thinks of Jesus.

The centurion says, “Surely this was a righteous man.” That's a Roman officer, standing right there, saying it out loud. Remember what the second criminal said earlier, that Jesus had done nothing wrong. Two different men, same kind of statement.
He says the exact opposite. The centurion says, “Surely this was a righteous man.” Guilty is not what comes out of his mouth. He gives glory to God and calls Jesus righteous.
That's not his word. The centurion says, “Surely this was a righteous man.” He doesn't call Him dangerous. He gives glory to God first, and then he says that.
Nobody's cheering, friend. Luke says the people who gathered “returned home beating their breasts.” I think that tells us the day hit them hard. Quiet walk home, no cheering.

Right, no cheering at all. Luke says that when the people who had gathered saw what happened, “they returned home beating their breasts.” I think it shows they walked home shaken. Luke doesn't say more about what was going through their minds.

Luke says all those who knew Jesus, including the women who had followed Him from Galilee, “stood at a distance watching these things.” They didn't leave. They stayed and watched. I think that says a lot about them.
That's what the crowd does. The people who gathered returned home beating their breasts. But the ones who knew Jesus are different. They stood at a distance watching.
Galilee is where those women followed Him from, so it's an easy guess. But Luke doesn't say anybody heads back there. He says they “stood at a distance watching these things.” They stayed put.
